title: Check the traceback starting from the last line.
body: A traceback shows the flow of the program from top to bottom where the error occurred.
detail: Beginners should first check the error type and message on the last line, and then work their way back up through the file and line numbers. The last line usually displays the error type—such as `ValueError` or `TypeError`—along with a human-readable message. Then, by following the `File` and `line` information at the top, you can narrow down where the problem originated—in which file and on which line.

title: "File" and "line" are clues for finding the location to correct.
body: A lower traceback frame is a strong clue to where the exception was detected, but that line is not guaranteed to be the root cause.
detail: Read the final exception type and message, then move upward through your code to find where the bad input originated.

title: `raise` intentionally raises an error
body: `raise` is a syntax that directly throws an exception when it detects problematic input or a problematic state.
detail: Instead of silently proceeding, it halts the execution flow and reveals the cause, leaving a clue for debugging. For example, if a score is negative, it may be safer to raise a `ValueError` to indicate that the input is invalid rather than continuing with the calculation. `raise` is not a syntax that annoys users; it is a mechanism that prevents the code from proceeding in an incorrect state.

title: "Finally" is often used in cleanup tasks.
body: finally runs cleanup during normal completion, handled exceptions, and ordinary control transfers such as return. It cannot guarantee execution after every forced process termination.
detail: A resource-specific context manager such as with is often simpler for files.

title: The "except" clause should be as specific as possible.
body: A specific except handles only failures the code expects and can recover from. A bare except also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, hiding stops and bugs.
detail: If recovery is impossible, preserve the traceback by re-raising after any necessary logging.

title: If you silently suppress errors, debugging becomes more difficult.
body: If you do nothing inside the `except` block or return a meaningless value, you may miss the actual cause. You need to log the reason for the failure or reproduce it so that you can track down the same problem later.
detail: Beginners often assume a problem is solved simply because the error is no longer displayed on the screen. However, if you move on without documenting the cause, it becomes difficult to trace the issue later when data is missing or results appear abnormal. You need to consider logging, error messages, and strategies for handling recurrence together.
